interest: This document provides a concise view into how pre-World War II commercial and military observation requests were handled by the State Department under classification 894.22711 (admission of foreigners to military institutions and industrial workshops). It is particularly interesting for capturing the transition from early 1930s military intelligence-sharing—where Japan raised no objection to a U.S. Army Air Service observation visit by Major B. Duty—to private commercial technical inspections on the eve of wider conflict in July 1937, when All America Cables executive John K. Roosevelt required diplomatic facilitation to inspect submarine cable manufacturing in Osaka right as the Second Sino-Japanese War broke out. It also illustrates the administrative mechanics of U.S. commercial diplomacy, including the billing of private corporations for consular telegraphic expenses.
overview: This file consists of a Department of State List of Papers (Form DS-46) under decimal file 894.22711, indexing records concerning the admission of United States nationals to military institutions, military aviation facilities, and industrial manufacturing plants in Japan between 1930 and 1937. The sheet records five documents (sub-numbers 14 through 18). Sub-number 14, dated January 3, 1930, notes that the Japanese government had no objection to a proposed visit by U.S. Army Major B. Duty to observe activities of the Japanese Army Air Service. Sub-numbers 15 through 18, dated July 20–28, 1937, track official assistance provided to John K. Roosevelt of All America Cables, Inc., coordinating with the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo and the U.S. Consulate at Osaka to obtain permission and documentation for him to enter and inspect an Osaka factory manufacturing submarine cables for purchase by his firm.

Documents 15 through 18 from July 1937 document arrangements coordinated by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs and the U.S. Consulate at Osaka on behalf of John K.
